On Wed, 10 May 2000, Sorrow wrote:

I didn't mean to include discarded cards in the set of unplayed cards. A
better term would be undrawn cards. When a methuselah is ousted there is
a set of undrawn cards. All random DLS does is blindly manipulate the set
of undrawn cards, putting some of them in the ash heap, without actually
changing the number of cards that go undrawn, and hence, without changing
a player's overall odds of drawing particular cards.

> However, if DLS is what caused the discard, it could have been
> something that would have been very useful to that player at the time
> but will now not have the opportunity to use it unless they happen to
> draw another.

Since you are ousting your prey before you run him out of cards, what if
instead of burning cards, DLS moved them to the bottom of the deck? They
will never draw those cards, so the effect is just as strong, stronger
even since they don't know which cards they are "losing" and can't revise
their plans accordingly. But does this affect their game? Of course not
- you are just blindly cutting their deck.

> > you don't know if you are getting rid of good stuff or getting rid of bad
> > stuff and letting them draw their good stuff sooner.
>
> Maybe, maybe not. Let's just take the following hypothetical situation:
>
> My prey's deck includes 4, say, Freak Drives. FD is somewhat critical
> to any strategy in that it allows vamps to take multiple actions per
> turn. Having FD could allow a vamp to, say, 5th, FD, Bleed. For every
> FD I eat away with DLS, that is one fewer action that can be performed
> utilizing the same resources.

But you have no conrtol over which cards get DLS'ed! That's why their
odds of drawing certain cards don't change - see my example below.

> All cards are in a players deck for a reason unless they were just
> thrown together. Each of those cards that goes unused (especially
> when it is not of the players choice) is a card that cannot be used to
> further that players position.

But there will always be cards which go unused if you are ousted with
library remaining - every card you didn't draw goes unused. DLS doesn't
make more unused cards; you still draw (are able to use) the same number
of cards in the course of the game. All the cards you don't draw always
go unused, whether DLS'ed or not.

> > They still draw the same number of cards before you oust them,
>
> Yes, but not in the same order or the same consistency (?; not sure if
> that's the right term) as they would have otherwise.

The order of cards is random - blindly rearranging them doesn't make them
any more or less random. The deck consistency *doesn't* change. The deck
is already inconsistent (having more Freak Drives on top than in the
middle or on the bottom.) You are just blindly manipulating which
inconsistent part they draw from. You are merely shuffling or cutting
their deck.

> > so their odds of drawing a particular set of cards are exactly the same
> > whether you use DLS or not.
>
> Not true. The odds change depending on how many of a particular card
> they include in the deck and how many DLS are used against them during
> the game. If the above player includes 4 FDs in their deck and I eat
> 3 of them with DLS, the odds of that player drawing the 4th aren't
> overly great. And if I eat the 4th FD with another DLS, then they
> just lost all of their FDs and it wasn't of their choosing.

It doesn't matter - if they still have a library, the overall odds of
drawing a Freak drive in the course of a game, DLS or not, remain the
same. Your odds of not DLS'ing a particular card combined with their
increased odds of drawing it exactly equals the original odds of drawing
that card.
Consider this hypothetical situation with a standard deck of
playing cards. Suppose we have a bet that I can shuffle the cards and
draw the ace of spades. We know the odds are of course 1/52. What are
the odds if you remove the top 26 cards before I draw? Half the time, you
will win right then and there, with the ace in your half. The other half
the time, the ace will be in the remaining 26 cards, so the odds of
drawing the ace from those cards is 1/26. Thus the overall odds are
1/2 * 1/26 = 1/52, exactly as before. In fact, you can remove between
zero and 51 cards and the odds of drawing the ace remains 1/52. The only
thing that changes is that we can know before I draw whether I have a shot
or not, which is why I claim that random DLS does nothing but demoralize
your opponent, without changing their chances of drawing what they want,
unless you actually run them out of cards.

-davey!

Missing the point slightly, I believe.

It's not that you have removed a significant portion of their blood
gain by dumping a Minion Tap in their ash heap. (although you may
have, if the deck only packs 5 Minion Taps.) You certainly can't
control which cards you get, but you CAN get lucky and get his good
ones. Good ones should be obvious - if an Awe and Dreams of the
Sphinx hit the heap, for example, the benefit is enormous.

It's that both your opponent *AND YOU* know that a Minion Tap is in
the ash heap and will NEVER be drawn. Your opponent may well be
completely demoralized and alter his style of play (he might know
there are only 4 in the deck, and with 1 in his hand and 1 in the
heap, he ain't likely to see more for a long time). You, however,
know that some of his blood gain is gone, and can alter your game
appropriately.

What if you see two Majesties vanish? That's information of a
different sort. Now he's out some combat defense. He may not be able
to recklessly bleed his prey as much, relying on Majesty to stop and
untap. He may not be able to multiple-block your bleeds with one or
two vampires since he can't untap as often anymore. You should alter
your game as much as you can (which may not be much given that you're
a DLS deck) to attack that weak point.

The purpose of a DLS deck isn't to run your prey out of cards, it's to
rob his deck of flow. If his deck is rolling well and suddenly you
jerk a few Bum's Rushes from the top onto the ash heap, he may not be
able to get into combat for several rounds. He might have been
waiting for the Rush actions which are now further down. A lot of
these things are "might"s, but don't ever underestimate them.

-- Derek

key card in my deck, say a Misdirection, my odds of drawing it depend ONLY
on the number of cards I draw in the course of the game and the *initial*
size of my deck. DLS doesn't change the initial deck size, and it doesn't
change the number of cards I draw until I run out of cards, which is an

misdirection are unchanged.

which cards Dirty Little Secrets burns, and the prey of a heavy bleed deck
seldom reaches the bottom of their library, would DLS not be just as
effective if it burned cards off the bottom of their deck? If not, why
not? If so, then how does DLS change their odds of drawing particular
cards if you don't run them out of cards?

> Unless you plan on bleeding them for 30+ pool (at which point you
> prolly should have ousted them),

> That's why I liked the Ani/Pro Seven Raptor deck idea better. You can

opponent's hand, not his deck, and the deck cycling can potentially run

game by running you out of cards before you were ousted or won. Maybe

How about let's actually do the math instead of just writing nonsense, eh?
If I have D cards left in my deck, the odds that I draw a particular card
are of course 1/D. What happens if you Dirty Little Secrets away X cards
at random first?

The revised odds of drawing the particular card =
(odds it was burned by DLS * 0)
+ (odds it was not burned * odds of drawing it from the reduced deck)

The odds it was burned is X/D
The odds it was not burned is thus 1 - (X/D) = (D - X)/D
The odds of drawing it from the reduced deck is 1/(size of reduced deck)
The size of the reduced deck is (D - X)

Thus my odds of drawing a particular card after you play Dirty Little
Secrets is: ((X/D) * 0) + ((D - X)/D * 1/(D - X)) = 0 + 1/D = 1/D
...exactly the same as if you never played the Dirty Little Secrets.

The only exception is when my deck is entirely gone; of course then my
chances of drawing the particular card are nil. But based on how DLS
works, this a highly unlikely circumstance.

2) The odds of him not drawing a Hungry Coyote in the course of the game
are not changed by your playing DLS.

3) The change in playstyle you describe is actually BAD for you.
Remember that sometimes the Tzimisce deck will fail to draw a Hungry
Coyote on its own. This has nothing to do with DLS, it's just the way the
game is - including only 2 copies a certain card means that some games you
won't ever see it. A good player understands this and after waiting for
key cards for what seems long enough, he will begin to alter his playstyle
accordingly, knowing that e.g. the Hungry Coyote has failed to provide the
benefit intended by its inclusion. In other words, he realizes his
initial playstyle is inappropriate and hence is causing him a
disadvantage. You want him to realize this as late as possible to
maximize the effect of this disadvantage.
By playing DLS, you don't actually increase his odds of getting a
bad draw, but when he does have a bad draw, your DLS gives him information
as to what kind of bad draw it will be, before he would have reached such
conclusions himself. Thus he is able to adopt his inevitable change in
playstyle earlier in the game, which means less of his game is played
incorrectly! Adapting one's playstyle is something good players do to get
the most out of their decks. Burning cards with DLS allows your opponent
to do this more rapidly and more effectively, essentially making him a
better player, and meanwhile it does nothing for you. This is not a good
thing for you.

Put another way, if you have ever had a bad draw, and thought to
yourself "If only I had known a few turns ago that I wasn't going to draw
my Hungry Coyote," Dirty Little Secrets provides just that kind of
information.

>have done some good. In Magic, that's pretty much the whole point the
>whole point of a Millstone. Unless someone points out and interesting
>combination, I would say the same is true here as well.

I suspect that lack of one card loses you a game FAR more often than
gaining just the right card wins you a VP or game.

That said, an interesting combination would be Scrying of Secrets and
Dirty Little Secrets - both action modifiers, so could be played on
the same action in sequence. Night Moves/Spying Mission/Computer
Hacking would get you the bleeds of 3 or 4 that are appropriate in
this case - since you can opt *not* to play DLS if you see that a
Deflection is, say, five cards down in his library. Inferior AUS is
all that is needed for SoS, so skill cards work here, and Kendrick
comes with inferior AUS already (and Kendrick rules.)

I'll poke with it a bit, but I think it could be very well utilized to
deliberately burn GOOD cards.
